Glossary — every term, simply Patta land Land for which a private owner holds a government-issued title record. Example: an ordinary farmer with a clean revenue record along the Musi’s middle reaches is a patta landowner under this scheme. Buffer zone A protective strip of land just outside a water body’s Full Tank Level, kept free of construction to protect its ecology and absorb flood flow. Example: land here gets 800 sq yards/acre under today’s scheme, less than ordinary patta land further from the river. Full Tank Level (FTL) The highest water level a lake or river stretch is engineered to hold. Example: land inside this line is legally meant to stay open for water, which is why its pooling return (400 sq yards/acre) is the smallest among patta categories. Encroachment land Land occupied or built on without a valid title, often riverbed or government land settled informally over time. Example: occupants here get 300 sq yards/acre — something, but the least of any category, reflecting their weaker legal claim. Transferable Development Rights (TDR) A certificate given to a landowner who surrenders land, letting them build extra floor area on a different plot they own, or sell that right to someone else (often a builder) instead of taking cash or a returned plot. Example: a buffer-zone owner here can choose TDR instead of the 800 sq-yard allotment. Land pooling vs. land acquisition Acquisition takes your land and pays fixed compensation under law; pooling takes your land TEMPORARILY, develops the whole area with roads and services, and gives you back a smaller, serviced plot from the same pooled land — the return ratio is set by whichever order governs that specific project, not by one universal rule. Example: today’s Musi ratios are one such project-specific pooling order, distinct from HMDA’s separate 60:40 one. 60:40 land-pooling ratio (HMDA) HMDA’s own standard scheme returns landowners roughly 60% of the value created (in practice, cited elsewhere as around 1,741 sq yards of developed plot per acre pooled), keeping 40% to sell and fund infrastructure. Example: this is the benchmark today’s Musi scheme is explicitly reported as NOT following. Multiple Use Zone A Master Plan land-use tag permitting a mix of residential, commercial and other uses on one parcel, rather than restricting it to a single use. Example: plots returned under this scheme carry this tag, which generally helps resale value and future construction flexibility. Master Plan A local or metropolitan authority’s official, legally-binding zoning map and rulebook, setting out what each area of land may be used for. Example: the "Multiple Use Zone" classification above is a Master Plan designation. Change-of-land-use (CLU) / land-use conversion charge A fee payable when a parcel’s officially recorded use (e.g. agricultural) is formally changed to another use (e.g. residential/commercial). Example: today’s scheme has the implementing entity, not the landowner, bear this charge on the plots handed back. Nala A natural or man-made storm-water drainage channel. Example: "nala charges" in this scheme relate to drainage-related costs on patta land, which the implementing entity is absorbing rather than passing to owners. Stamp duty A state tax paid on registering a property transaction, usually calculated as a percentage of the property’s market value. Example: Telangana’s normal combined stamp duty and registration charge runs close to 6% on an ordinary sale; this scheme fixes it at just 0.5% for plots returned to landowners — a real, quantifiable sweetener. Restriction periods run 10–20 years by scheme — counted from the ALLOTMENT date, not from when the current seller acquired it. SC/ST-assigned land never loses its restriction. Buyers get pulled into CB-CID cases as often as sellers: registering a deed on restricted land counts as participation, intent or not. IPC 420, 465, 468 and 471 recur in these charge sheets — and 420 is NON-BAILABLE. 2C patta (converted-for-residential land) and assigned patta are DIFFERENT things — agents blur them, and that blur alone has put buyers in front of investigators. The patta’s remarks column and the A-Register hold everything you need — read both before any advance. What assigned patta actually is It reads like any other patta — survey number, name, extent, classification. The difference hides in a clause in the REMARKS section, or in the assignment order sitting behind the patta that sellers do not always show. Governments have allotted land to landless families, SC/ST beneficiaries, ex-servicemen and other eligible groups under welfare schemes — and the original assignment order carries the real terms: how long the beneficiary must hold, what the land may be used for, and whether government approval is needed before any sale. What the conditions mean in practice Restriction periods commonly run 10–20 years depending on the scheme — counted from the DATE OF ALLOTMENT, not from whenever the current seller took over. Violate them and the government cancels the patta and takes the land back — no warning, no compensation. The person who paid full market price is left with nothing, and on record the sale is treated as if it never legally happened. Why purchases turn into CID cases The script is always the same: a seller holds assigned land still inside its restriction period; the buyer is told the patta is clean or the condition “doesn’t apply anymore”; money moves, the deed registers. Then — sometimes years later — a neighbour complains or a revenue officer notices something during routine inspection. The Tahsildar orders an inquiry, confirms the violation, and the case moves to the police — often the CB-CID. The buyer’s registered deed is not a defence; it is EXHIBIT A. The criminal sections that get invoked IPC 420 — cheating by dishonest inducement, up to seven years, and NON-BAILABLE: arrest can precede a magistrate’s order. IPC 465 — forgery, where patta records were altered or a condition quietly omitted. IPC 468 — forgery for the purpose of cheating. IPC 471 — USING a forged document as genuine — the section that can reach a buyer who registered a deed without ever checking its underlying conditions. This is the lesson’s hardest truth: in assigned-land cases the buyer is treated as a participant, not merely a victim. 2C patta ≠ assigned patta 2C patta : agricultural land formally CONVERTED for residential use — its one condition (agricultural classification) already resolved through a conversion order. No welfare distribution behind it, no community restriction, no lock-in on sale. Assigned patta : welfare redistribution, with conditions on who may own, how long they must hold, and whether it can be sold at all. Agents in a hurry blur the two — and that blur alone has put buyers in front of investigators. If a seller says “2C”, verify it is a CONVERSION story, not an ASSIGNMENT story: the paper trail behind each is completely different. Example: A buyer is shown a “2C patta — fully converted, free to sell”. The A-Register extract tells another story: allotted 2011 under a housing scheme to an SC beneficiary — an assignment, restriction unexpired and, being SC-assigned, never expiring. The “conversion” framing was the con. One ₹50 counter application at the revenue office exposed it. How to verify before you pay ☐ Pull the LATEST patta/ownership record from the state portal. ☐ Get the A-REGISTER extract (or state equivalent) at the revenue office — it shows the original allotment date and scheme. ☐ Compute the restriction period from the ALLOTMENT date, not the seller’s purchase date. ☐ SC/ST-assigned? The restriction does not expire — check buyer eligibility before going one step further. ☐ Even past the window, some schemes require written Collector permission before registration — confirm. ☐ Review the ownership history: a pattern of quick, repeated transfers is exactly what CB-CID investigations flag. Quick answers (FAQ) Can assigned patta land be sold legally? Only where the scheme’s conditions allow — restriction expired, permissions obtained, or formal de-restriction granted. The non-alienation period? 10–20 years by scheme, from allotment; perpetual for SC/ST assignments. Why do BUYERS end up in cases? Because registering a deed on restricted land is treated as participation in the violation. If conditions are violated? Cancellation, resumption without compensation — plus the criminal exposure above. Bottom line This is the one land category where a mistake is not just money — it is a charge sheet. The remarks column and the A-Register cost minutes and rupees to read; read them before any advance, and walk away from any seller who resists the reading. A chartered accountant issues Form 15CB confirming capital-gains tax is paid. 4. Submit Form 15CA online with the sale deed and bank statements. 5. The bank verifies, converts, remits. Not one bank visit — a CA, a bank and the tax department all signing off; budget weeks, not days. Red flags Cash, or any channel outside normal banking — an outright FEMA violation; every rupee must move through banks. Skipped or botched 15CA/15CB filings — transfers block. Repatriation limits by funding route How the property was funded What can leave India The cap that applies NRE / FCNR (foreign funds) Full sale proceeds Two residential properties per LIFETIME; beyond that, RBI approval NRO account / Indian income Proceeds via NRO USD 1 million per financial year, any property count Bought while a resident Proceeds via NRO USD 1 million per year Inherited property Proceeds via NRO USD 1 million per year + inheritance proof + tax clearance Foreign funding suits a buyer who will sell at most two properties in a lifetime. Only to full repatriation of foreign-funded RESIDENTIAL purchases; the annual cap governs the rest. 2026-10-02|ls-capital-gains: Capital gains tax on agricultural land sale Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: Capital Gains Tax on Agricultural Land Sale in India — 1acre.in Key Highlights Rural agricultural land is NOT a capital asset under Section 2(14)(iii) — its sale attracts no capital gains tax at all. The rural test is mechanical: the nearest municipality’s census population, and aerial distance of 2 / 6 / 8 km. Urban agricultural land is taxed like any property; long-term starts at 24 months. Section 54B exemption needs TWO years of actual farming before sale, reinvestment in farmland within two years, and a three-year lock-in on the new land. Section 50C lets the taxman substitute the stamp-duty value when you sell below it. When the tax applies at all One question decides everything: is the land RURAL or URBAN under the Income Tax Act? Rural agricultural land is excluded from the very definition of a capital asset by Section 2(14)(iii) — no capital asset, no capital gain, nothing to tax. Urban agricultural land gets no carve-out and is taxed like any other asset. Two owners can sell what looks like the same plot and one pays nothing while the other owes tax on the whole gain — purely because of where the land sits. The rural test — mechanical, not agricultural Nothing to do with how the land is farmed; everything to do with location and population. Land is RURAL if it lies outside a municipality or cantonment of 10,000+ people, AND outside these aerial distances from those limits: 2 km where the population is 10,000–1 lakh; 6 km where it is 1–10 lakh; 8 km where it exceeds 10 lakh. Population comes from the last published census; distance is measured AERIALLY — as the crow flies, not as the road winds. Inside the limits = urban agricultural land = taxable. One nuance: the exemption attaches to the LAND — a farmhouse, well or standing trees sold in the same deal are valued and treated separately. Example: Two farmers sell near Hyderabad (population >10 lakh, so the 8 km band applies). One’s land sits 9 km aerially from the municipal limit — rural, gain fully exempt. The other’s sits 7 km out — urban, fully taxable. Same crop, same buyer profile, two kilometres of geometry worth lakhs in tax. The second test: was it actually farmed? Classification decides the tax; CULTIVATION decides whether your claim survives scrutiny. Revenue records carry seasonal cultivation entries — the evidence that agricultural operations actually happened — and Section 54B leans on exactly that record for its two-year farming condition. Land held bare as pure investment is where exemption claims die at assessment. How the gain is computed Sale price minus purchase cost and expenses. Held 24+ months: long-term. The current long-term regime taxes gains at 12.5% without indexation (indexation having been withdrawn for post-July-2024 sales). And Section 50C looms over the price itself: sell below the stamp-duty value and the department can treat THAT value as your deemed sale price, subject to a tolerance margin — the guideline value quietly setting your tax floor. Rural vs urban at a glance Aspect Rural agricultural land Urban agricultural land Capital asset? No — s.2(14)(iii) excludes it Yes Capital gains tax None LTCG/STCG as applicable TDS on sale (194-IA) Expressly excluded 1% at ₹50 lakh+ (resident seller) Exemption routes Not needed 54B (farmland), 54EC (bonds) The exits: 54B and 54EC Section 54B — individuals and HUFs: reinvest the gain in NEW agricultural land within two years, provided the sold land was farmed for the two years before sale; money not yet reinvested by the return-filing date parks in a Capital Gains Account Scheme; the new land locks in for three years — sell early and the exemption unwinds. Section 54EC — the alternative for long-term gains: NHAI/REC/PFC/IRFC bonds within six months (₹50 lakh cap, five-year lock). The taxes that ride alongside TDS: buyers deduct 1% under 194-IA on urban agricultural land at ₹50 lakh+ — rural land is expressly outside the section. NRI sellers: Section 195 instead, at much higher rates — plan with a lower-deduction certificate. 50C: as above, the stamp-value floor. Quick answers (FAQ) Is rural agricultural land exempt? Fully — it is not a capital asset. How is “rural” defined? The census-population + aerial-distance test above. Indexation still available? Not under the current 12.5% regime. Urban land exemptions? 54B with the farming and lock-in conditions; 54EC bonds. TDS on farmland? Urban yes (₹50L+), rural no. Don’t want to buy farmland again? 54EC bonds, or pay the 12.5% and stay liquid. Bottom line Before selling any farmland, establish three things in writing: the aerial distance to the nearest 10,000+ municipality, the census figure that sets the band, and the cultivation record. Those three lines decide whether the tax is zero, exempt-with-conditions, or fully payable — get a CA’s letter where kilometres decide lakhs. For you: For your JD landowner partners this is THE conversation: many Ranga Reddy parcels sit inside Hyderabad’s 8 km band — urban, taxable — while one village further out is exempt. Knowing which side of the line a family’s land falls (and flagging 54B’s two-year farming condition early) makes you the developer who saved them lakhs before the deal even signed. 2026-10-02|ls-nri-guide: NRI guide to buying land in India: rules, restrictions, and what to know Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: NRI Guide to Buying Land in India: Rules, Restrictions, and What to Know Before You Invest — 1acre.in Key Highlights Residential and commercial property: NRIs buy freely — no cap, no RBI approval. Agricultural land, farmhouses and plantations: banned under FEMA, with three narrow exceptions. Repatriating sale money depends on FEMA rules, where the purchase money came from, and tax compliance. Long-term gains (held 24+ months) now taxed at 12.5% WITHOUT indexation — and NRIs miss the grandfathering relief residents got. Buying from abroad is an information problem: due diligence must happen BEFORE the wire, not after. Who counts as an NRI here The definitions run through FEMA, 1999. An NRI is an Indian citizen living abroad — Indian passport overseas. An OCI is a foreign citizen of Indian origin — foreign passport, Indian roots. For property purchases the two follow essentially identical rules, so everything below applies to both. What NRIs can and cannot buy Freely: apartments, villas, houses, offices, shops — residential and commercial, any number, no RBI approval. Never: agricultural land, farmhouses, plantation property — a national ban, whatever the buyer’s income or country, and it covers every route: sale deed, agreement to sell, or any indirect structure trying to dress the purchase up. Why the farmland ban exists The restriction lives in FEMA’s capital-account framework — today the Non-debt Instruments Rules, 2019 plus the RBI Master Direction, not one neat section. The policy logic: farmland touches food security, and offshore money flooding in could distort prices and displace the people who actually work the land. RBI approval technically exists but is granted rarely, for genuine agricultural or public-interest cases — it is not an investment route. And breaking the rule is not a slap on the wrist: the transaction can be VOIDED, the Enforcement Directorate can step in, and penalties can reach three times the value. The three exceptions Inheritance — the common path: an NRI can inherit farmland from a resident Indian (or from another NRI with RBI clearance), and can later sell it — but only to a resident Indian. Gift from a specified relative — allowed if the giver is a RESIDENT Indian who qualifies as a specified relative under FEMA; NRI-to-NRI farmland gifting is barred. Prior ownership — farmland you owned while resident stays yours after your status changes; the ban bites only on NEW acquisitions. In all three cases, sending the eventual sale money abroad is not automatic — RBI guidance and tax compliance govern it. The buying process, step by step 1) Confirm eligibility — your NRI/OCI status, and that the property is residential/commercial, not agricultural or plantation. 2) Shortlist RERA-registered projects and verify approvals with the authority. 3) Due diligence — 30-year title search plus EC, ruling out disputes, mortgages and legally non-transferable land. 4) Open the NRI account — NRE, NRO or FCNR; every rupee routes through it (cash is barred under FEMA and tax law alike). 5) Execute a PoA if you will not attend — embassy-attested or apostilled in Hague-convention countries, then stamped in India before use. 6) Sign the agreement on stamp paper with a payment schedule; register within four months. 7) Transfer funds and KEEP the Foreign Inward Remittance Certificate. 8) Pay stamp duty at the state’s rate. 9) Register the sale deed — in person or via the PoA holder — this is the ownership proof. 10) Afterwards: file tax on any rent, and keep records seven years. Definition — NRE / NRO / FCNR: the three NRI bank accounts. NRE holds foreign earnings (fully repatriable), NRO holds Indian earnings (repatriation capped), FCNR holds foreign-currency deposits. WHICH account funded the purchase decides how freely the sale money can leave later. Repatriation — getting money out later From an NRO account, up to USD 1 million per financial year can go abroad, subject to tax compliance. Property bought with FOREIGN funds via NRE: full repatriation of sale proceeds, for up to two residential properties; beyond two, the money joins the USD-1-million pipeline. Bought with NRO (India-earned) money: capped and paperwork-heavy. The lesson runs backwards in time: the repatriation freedom you want at EXIT is decided by the account you use at ENTRY. Example: Two NRIs each sell a Hyderabad flat for ₹2 crore. One bought via NRE with dollars — proceeds wire out cleanly. The other bought with NRO rupees — the same money now queues under the annual cap with Forms 15CA/15CB. Identical flats; the funding route made the difference. Documents you will need Identity: passport (with OCI card if applicable), PAN, proof of overseas residence. Property: title deed with 30-year history, EC, regulatory approvals, and for completed buildings the approved plan and occupancy certificate. Transaction: NRI-account statements, the FIRC, the attested PoA if buying in absentia, and Forms 15CA/15CB where remittances abroad cross ₹5 lakh a year. Tax obligations TDS turns on who SELLS: buy from a resident and TDS is the small 1% over ₹50 lakh; buy from another NRI and TDS applies at much higher rates regardless of value. Capital gains: property held over 24 months is long-term, taxed at 12.5% — and NRIs do NOT get the grandfathered indexation relief residents kept, so old purchases can carry surprisingly large taxable gains. Rent earned in India is taxed in India (standard deduction applies); tax treaties usually let you credit Indian tax against the home-country bill. Buying from a distance — the real risk The hardest part of absentee buying is the gap between what a listing claims and what the land is. Map overlays and verified survey numbers narrow that gap — classification, zoning, boundary, location — before you wire an advance or fly in. But no map reads a title chain, catches a forged deed, or gives FEMA and tax advice: a property lawyer and a tax advisor who handle NRI transactions remain non-negotiable, because a wrong classification does not just lose money — it can void the transaction. Quick answers (FAQ) Can an NRI buy restricted or assigned land? No — the assigned-land bans apply on top of FEMA. Any cap on how many properties? No cap on residential/commercial ownership; repatriation rules differ beyond two. Buy without visiting India? Yes — via a properly attested and stamped PoA. Sell inherited farmland? Yes, but only to a resident Indian. What if an NRI buys farmland in breach? Transaction voidable, ED proceedings, penalty up to 3× the value. Bottom line The rules are clear on paper and unforgiving in practice. Confirm the land’s classification BEFORE committing, route every payment through the right NRI account, and put a lawyer and tax advisor on the file — the two costs that are always cheaper than the mistake. For you: NRI money is a major buyer pool for Hyderabad plots — and every NRI buyer’s first fear is exactly this lesson. A venture that hands NRI buyers a ready file (residential classification proof, RERA number, PoA template, TDS guidance) converts that fear into sales.
